Spruce budworm flight phenology in Maine

Daily dynamics — analysis log

Author

JN Candau

Published

1 October 2026

1 Purpose of this document

This is the running log of the analyses of spruce budworm (Choristoneura fumiferana) flight phenology from daily light-trap catches in Maine. Each section records what was done, the choices that were made and why, and the state of the data or the model that resulted. It is updated as the work proceeds; the numbers below are recomputed from the processed data every time the document is rendered, so they cannot drift away from the files on disk.

Code lives in R/, source data in data/raw/, processed tables in data/processed/. The project is version-controlled at https://github.com/jncandau/Maine_Oct_2026.

Project layout. This log documents the Daily dynamics analysis: the night-by-night distribution of catches. It shares its dataset with a second analysis, Seasonal dynamics (seasonal_dynamics/). The data layer is common to both and sits at the project root — R/01_read_trap_data.R, R/02_read_weather_data.R, the two development-model runs R/03_biosim_phenology.R and R/04_pupal_phenology.R, R/functions/phenology.R and data/. The scripts cited here as R/05 to R/14 and R/functions/predict_flight.R live under daily_dynamics/R/.

2 Trap data

2.1 Source

The captures come from the eastern spruce budworm phenology dataset of Fournier, Candau et al. (2027), held in the private repository jncandau/SBWFieldPhenoDatabase and copied unmodified into data/raw/SBWFieldPhenoDatabase/. The workbook Eastern Spruce Budworm Phenology V1.ods holds three tables — Phenology, Flight and References — joined by referenceID. Only Flight is used here.

Flight is a wide table: one row per trapping record, with the captures of each night in the columns mothsDay160 … mothsDay231 (day of year 160 to 231). A record is a site × year × sampling method × sex combination, and carries its coordinates, the reported season total mothCountYear, and a pointer to the source publication. Across North America it holds 763 records; Maine contributes 643 light-trap records and 36 yard-light records.

2.2 Reading and decoding

R/01_read_trap_data.R reads the sheet with every column forced to character, because the day columns mix numbers with two text codes:

The two codes are not equivalent. m marks a night that was sampled and whose value is lost, and it stays missing. - carries no count at all, and what it means depends on when it falls: inside the flight season the trap was running and caught nothing, which is a zero; outside it the trap was not operating and the night does not exist.

The season of a year is therefore defined once, from the catches themselves: it runs from the first to the last night on which any trap in the dataset caught a moth that year. Every record of that year is expanded to that window — its own counts where it has them, zeros on the - nights, NA on the m nights — and anything outside the window is dropped. n_zero_filled records how many nights each record owes to this rule.

This is a modelling decision with teeth. It asserts that a trap with no entry for a mid-season night was running and empty, which turns roughly half of all nights in the dataset into informative zeros and means no record is truncated by construction: a trap that was in fact installed late is now credited with zeros it never recorded.

The wide table is then pivoted to one row per record-night, and a calendar date is derived from the year and the day of year.

2.3 Selection

Four criteria define the working dataset, all set as constants at the top of R/01_read_trap_data.R:

The year window drops 1961–1967 and 2016. The catch threshold removes a further 230 in-window records; it also removes, without needing a separate rule, every record that reports only a season total and no daily series, and all of 1963–1967 and 2016, where no trap anywhere in Maine exceeded 99 moths.

2.4 Pooling of sex-split records

Two 1980 localities report the male and the female catch of one trap as separate records. Since the trap is the sampling unit, the pairs are summed night by night before the catch threshold is applied, and the components are removed. Both pairs sampled identical nights with no missing values, so the sums are exact.

Pooling matters beyond tidiness: at Bare Island neither sex reached the threshold alone (83 and 78 moths) but the trap caught 161, so the locality re-enters the dataset.

2.5 The resulting dataset

Two tables are written to data/processed/:

  • trap_records.rds — one row per trapping record, with sampling effort, season total and provenance;
  • trap_daily.rds — one row per record-night that was inside a trapping season, holding the count and its status.

The network is a rotating panel rather than a fixed set of stations: most localities contribute a handful of years, and the annual number of traps varies with the outbreak and with the Maine Forest Service’s programme.

2.5.1 Data quality

The following checks are run by R/01_read_trap_data.R at every read. They report problems; they never repair them.

Of the 8,286 counted nights, 2,720 are zeros supplied by this rule and 50% of all counted nights caught nothing. Only 30 nights remain missing, all of them m codes inside a season window; the large June blocks of m codes in 1982 and 1983 fall before the first capture of their year and so leave the dataset with the rest of the out-of-season range.

2.6 Minimum effort for phenology

A season total above 99 moths says nothing about whether the trap was running long enough, or at the right time, to describe a flight curve. The rule below matches the requirement to the statistic: for a percentile to be identifiable, the sampling window has to bracket it. If more than 5% of a season’s catch falls on the first night, the 5th percentile sits at or before that night and cannot be located; the same argument applies to p95 and the last night.

The criteria are recorded, not enforced: trap_records carries coverage, tail_first, tail_last and the logical usable_phenology, so an analysis that needs only the median can relax them.

Effort itself is rarely the problem: coverage is exactly 1 for most records and the median series runs 25 nights. Truncation is what binds, and it is not a marginal call in the worst cases — East Allagash 1986 took 77% of its season on the final night, Round Mountain 1972 71% on the first.

The cost is concentrated in the sparse years. Sensitivity of the tail threshold, holding the other two criteria fixed:

1987 and 1988 have a single trap each, so one failing record erases the year. Whether that is acceptable depends on the analysis: a pooled site-year model loses little, a year-by-year trend loses the two terminal years of the outbreak collapse.

2.7 Open questions

  • 1987 and 1988 have no usable record. Under the current tail threshold both years disappear from the phenology set. Relaxing the threshold to 0.10 restores 1987 at the cost of admitting series whose flight period is probably truncated; the decision belongs with the analysis, not the reader.
  • Weather resolution. The CaSR reanalysis covers every retained locality (all within 6.3 km of a grid cell) and every retained year, but air temperature is stored 3-hourly, not hourly, unlike the other four variables.
  • Records excluded by the year window. 1961–1967 and 2016 are outside the reanalysis, and are set aside rather than lost: widening keep_years and setting min_season_total to 0 in R/01_read_trap_data.R restores the full 643-record Maine light-trap set.

3 Weather data

3.1 Source

Weather comes from the ECCC Canadian Surface Reanalysis (CaSR v3.2), a ~10 km rotated-pole reanalysis. The two tiles that cover Maine were downloaded from the CaSR download page into data/raw/Weather_Maine/ — 60 NetCDF files, 4.1 GB, five variables in six four-year periods spanning 1968–1991.

The reanalysis window is what fixes keep_years in the trap selection: 1968 is the first year with weather, and no trap in 1990 or 1991 was sampled.

3.2 Extraction

R/02_read_weather_data.R takes the locality-years from data/processed/trap_records.rds, projects the trap coordinates onto the rotated-pole grid, assigns each locality to the tile that contains it, and extracts the grid cell holding the trap for every hour of the calendar year.

Two details of the file layout needed care.

The period files are not aligned on calendar years. Each spans 31 December 13:00 UTC of the year before its period to 31 December 12:00 UTC of its last year, so the final 11 hours of 1971, 1975, 1979, 1983 and 1987 sit in the next period file. Selecting layers by year within a single file silently returns 8,749-hour years; the script reads both files for those years.

The tiles are read separately. Each locality is extracted from the one tile that covers it, rather than merging two 35,064-layer rasters per variable and period.

3.3 The resulting dataset

data/processed/weather_hourly.rds (51 MB) holds one row per locality-year with a nested Weather tibble: datetime (UTC), datetime_est (local standard time, UTC−5 all year), the interpolated Temp, the raw TT, and PR0, FB, P0, UVC.

3.3.1 Interpolation of air temperature

Temperature is stored every three hours, so two hours in three are filled with chillR::interpolate_gaps_hourly(), which fits an idealised daily temperature curve to the daily minima and maxima — hence the latitude argument — and interpolates the residuals. The measured values are left untouched, which is worth verifying rather than assuming:

The deviation at measured hours is floating-point noise, so Temp reproduces TT exactly where TT exists and only fills the gaps between.

3.3.2 Does the weather look like Maine?

Summer temperature falls towards the north, but latitude alone orders the localities poorly. The coolest Julys belong to coastal and island sites — Bare Island 17.2 °C at 44.6° N, Georgetown 17.4 °C at 43.8° N, Steuben 17.6 °C at 44.5° N — all cooler than Estcourt, 21.0 °C on the Québec border at 47.4° N. Any temperature-driven model of flight timing therefore has to carry the maritime gradient, not just latitude.

3.4 Open questions for the weather

  • Temperature is interpolated, not measured, for two hours in three. Any night-level analysis that depends on a specific hour — the temperature at dusk, or hours above a flight threshold — inherits the idealised diurnal curve, not the reanalysis. Aggregates over a whole night are much less exposed than instantaneous values.
  • Local time is a constant offset. datetime_est is UTC−5 all year, so it is one hour behind civil time in summer. A series nested by UTC year starts at 19:00 on 31 December of the preceding year in local time.
  • Reanalysis, not stations. CaSR is a model product on a 10 km grid: the cell holding a trap is 0.7–6.3 km from it and represents ~100 km², so the extracted series describes the neighbourhood, not the trap clearing.

4 Modelled phenology from BioSIM

Alongside the observed catches, spruce budworm seasonal biology was simulated at every trap locality-year with BioSIM, so that observed and modelled flight phenology can be compared on the same dates and the same statistic.

4.1 Model and weather

R/03_biosim_phenology.R calls the BioSIM Web API through the BioSIM R package, which drives a Java client. For each year one request covers the localities sampled that year: BioSIM assembles the daily weather for those coordinates from its own historical station network and runs Spruce_Budworm_Biology on it — Régnière’s process-oriented model of spruce budworm seasonal biology (Régnière 1982, 1983, 1984, 1987, 1990; Régnière & You 1991), driven by daily minimum, mean and maximum temperature.

This is a second, independent weather source: the CaSR reanalysis of the previous section is not what BioSIM uses. Every simulated day in this run came back marked as resting on observed rather than generated weather.

4.2 Parameters

The model takes eight parameters. Seven are left at the server defaults; the two mortality switches are turned off.

Mortality is off because the question here is when the stages occur, not how many survive. With mortality on, only a few percent of the cohort reaches the adult stage, so the flight curve would be estimated from a handful of individuals: checked at one Maine locality-year, the season totals are MaleEmergence + FemaleEmergence = 100% and MaleFlight + FemaleFlight = 97% with mortality off, against 10% and 6% under the defaults.

LastSampleDate and ObservedAI are left unset, so the simulations are driven by weather alone and are not anchored on any field observation of development.

4.3 What the model returns, and what is kept

The output is daily and everything is a percentage of the simulated cohort, quantised in steps of 0.25%. Besides the eight stages (L2o … Adults) it reports emergence, flight, oviposition and death, separately for each sex. Three quantities are kept, each the sum of the two sexes, and a fourth is derived from them:

Flight and pupation are daily fluxes, so their cumulative curves are genuine distributions over the season; flight is the series to compare with trap catches, pupation the one to compare with bayessbw. BioSIM does not report pupation directly. With mortality off, an individual that has pupated by a given day is either still a pupa or has already emerged, so cumulative pupation is the pupae present plus the cumulative emergence, and its daily increments are the pupation dates. The two stocks are weighted by how long individuals remain in the stage and are kept for context: the median of the pupal stock is the middle of the pupal period, not the date of pupation. The sex-specific columns reproduce the both-sexes columns the model also reports exactly, which is checked at every run.

The simulation is repeated ten times per locality-year and the runs are averaged, which smooths the 0.25% quantisation of a single run; percentiles are unaffected by the choice of averaging over summing.

4.4 The resulting dataset

Modelled flight is centred on day of year 190 on average — 9 July — and the central 90% of it spans a fortnight. Pupation runs about ten days ahead of flight, and the adult stock peaks slightly after flight because adults persist once mortality is switched off.

The locality-year medians are spread over six weeks (DOY 169 to 210) and all 227 values differ, so the simulations respond to site and year rather than returning a regional average: 1974 alone spans DOY 182 to 210 across its 21 localities.

4.5 Cohorts that do not finish

With mortality off, a locality-year should end with essentially the whole cohort having flown. Not all of them do: part of the cohort fails to complete development and is dropped, which shows up as a flight season total well below 100%. flight_complete marks the locality-years that reach at least 90%.

Two features of that list matter. It is concentrated at particular sites rather than scattered — Clayton Lake is flagged in five separate years — which points to a site effect rather than to bad years. And the flagged locality-years are later, not earlier, than the complete ones, which is the opposite of what one would expect if the surviving fraction were the fast developers; it is consistent instead with incompleteness arising in cold site-years where development runs late. The flag is carried on all three series and nothing is dropped: what to do with these locality-years is a decision for the analysis.

4.6 Open questions for the modelled phenology

  • The comparison with the catches is still to be done. On the three locality-years used to test the script, modelled flight ran one to two weeks ahead of the observed catch window; whether that holds over the whole run is the next question, and the two tables join on locality-year.
  • Three parameters are undocumented. ApplyAdultMortality, Defoliation and AdultLongevity have no description in the model help and no stated units. AdultLongevity = 0 in particular may be what makes the adult stock persist to the end of the year.
  • Nothing anchors the simulation to observed development. The model offers LastSampleDate and ObservedAI for that, and the Phenology sheet of the source workbook holds average-instar observations — none of them in Maine, but the option exists for a validation elsewhere.

5 Modelled pupation from bayessbw

A second, independent model of development was run over the same locality-years: the Bayesian development model of Studens et al. (kdis19/bayessbw), driven by the CaSR hourly temperatures of Section 3 rather than by BioSIM’s own weather.

5.1 What the model is, and what “pupal phenology” means here

bayessbw fits Sharpe-DeMichele / Schoolfield development-rate curves to laboratory rearing data, in a Bayesian hierarchical form: every posterior draw carries a rate curve for each larval stage plus a lognormal individual-variation term. The fitted posterior is distributed as the R package sbwFieldPheno, whose dev_days() accumulates development hour by hour through a temperature series and returns the day of year on which each simulated individual reaches a given stage.

The laboratory data stop at L6, so the model describes the five larval stages L2 to L6 only. Pupation is the end of L6 — the last transition the model knows about — and the pupal stage itself is not modelled. Pupal phenology here therefore means the date of pupation, not the duration of the pupal stage. This is also how bayessbw’s own weather simulations use the package.

R/04_pupal_phenology.R runs it with the settings below.

Two things about that table matter more than the rest. dev_days() starts accumulating development on the first row of weather it is given, so 1 March is an assumption about the date of post-diapause L2 emergence, and every predicted date moves with it. And because all 100 posterior draws are used, the posterior spread reported below is the model’s own uncertainty, not a sampling error.

5.2 The resulting dataset

Each simulation returns a matrix of individuals by posterior draws. Sorting a draw’s column turns it into that draw’s population distribution, and taking the median rank by rank across draws gives the median simulated population — the summary bayessbw itself uses, written out in full as pupal_population.rds. Percentiles in the table above are percentiles of that population; the posterior interval is built the other way round, from the median of each draw, so the two columns separate individual variation from parameter uncertainty.

They differ by a factor of four: the fitted curves place the population median to within about two days, while the population itself takes nine days to pupate from p05 to p95. Individual variation, not parameter uncertainty, dominates.

The two models were built from different data, fitted by different methods and driven by different weather. They agree on the pattern of pupation across locality-years (r = 0.78) but not on its date: BioSIM pupates a median 4.0 days earlier than bayessbw. Their disagreement at individual locality-years reaches two weeks in both directions, which is the scale at which either model’s site-level prediction should be trusted.

Correction (1 October 2026). Earlier versions of this log compared bayessbw with the median of BioSIM’s pupal stock and found the two within a day of each other. That median falls a median 4.9 days after BioSIM’s median pupation date, because a pupa is counted on every day it spends in the stage. The near-agreement was the pupal period offsetting the models’ real difference in pupation date.

5.3 Open questions for the pupation model

  • The 1 March start is an assumption, not a measurement. Anchoring the simulation on BioSIM’s own L2 emergence date instead would make the two models comparable on equal terms and remove one arbitrary choice.
  • One colony of six. NB is used throughout. The other five are one configuration change away, and comparing them would show how much the source population matters against site and year.
  • The pupal stage is not modelled. Getting from pupation to flight needs either BioSIM or a separate pupal development function; the section below measures that interval empirically instead.

6 Model versus observed

R/05_compare_model_observed.R brings the three sides together, one row per locality-year: the percentiles of the nightly catch curve, the percentiles of BioSIM’s daily flight curve, and the predicted date of pupation from both models. All of them are percentiles of a curve over the season computed by the same helper (R/functions/phenology.R), so p50 always means half of the season’s total has happened by this day.

6.1 What can be compared

A caught moth is not the same thing as a flying moth: the trap samples adults that are active, close enough and attracted to light, whereas BioSIM reports the percentage of the cohort in the flight state. The comparison below is about timing, never about numbers.

Two flags decide which rows carry a meaningful comparison, and both are kept in the output rather than filtered away.

Only the first group is used for the statistics that follow. The truncated seasons are shown in the table because their offset is the diagnostic one would expect: a season that starts too late or ends too early pushes the observed median towards the middle of the sampled window, and those rows sit further from the model than the comparable ones.

6.2 Flight

The model is early, but only just: half a day to four days, depending on which part of the curve is compared. That is a much smaller bias than the one to two weeks suggested by the three locality-years used to test the simulation script, and it settles the open question left at the end of Section 4.

The offset is largest at the start of the season and smallest at the end, which is another way of saying that the modelled flight period is longer than the observed one — 14.7 days against 11.0 between p05 and p95. Part of that is real and part is an artefact of trapping: a trap that catches nothing on a night when a few moths fly contributes nothing to the tails of the observed curve.

The average is not the whole story, though.

This is the substantive result of the comparison, and it has three parts.

Both models get the year right. Averaged over the localities sampled in a year, predicted and observed median dates correlate at 0.83 for BioSIM and 0.71 for bayessbw: warm early seasons and cold late ones are reproduced, and the six-week span of median flight dates across the record is not an artefact of which sites happened to be trapped.

Neither gets the site right. Once the year is removed, the correlation across localities within a year collapses to 0.14 for BioSIM and 0.06 for bayessbw. Whatever makes one Maine locality fly earlier than another in the same summer, neither model captures it.

The residual is not noise, and it is the same residual in both models. It has a clear spatial structure — the offset correlates with latitude at 0.49 (BioSIM) and 0.39 (bayessbw), so both run early in the south, and more weakly with the size of the catch (0.28 and 0.17; the two are disentangled below) — and the two models’ offsets correlate with each other at 0.74, locality-year by locality-year. That last number is the informative one. The models were fitted to different data by different methods and, crucially, were driven by different weather: BioSIM interpolates its own station network, bayessbw ran on the CaSR grid extracted in Section 3. A spatial error common to both is therefore unlikely to originate in either weather source. It points instead at something both models share — temperature-driven development with no site-level modifier — or at something neither of them contains, of which immigration is the obvious candidate.

The worst-fitting sites are southern and coastal — the same localities that the weather section found to have the coolest Julys in the dataset despite their latitude. A model that is too early there is a model whose development is running too fast on those temperature series. They are also the localities that catch the fewest moths, which is a second candidate explanation and is separated from latitude below.

6.3 From pupation to flight

The pupal stage is missing from bayessbw and the trap sees only adults, so the interval between them can be measured rather than modelled.

The median catch falls 13.4 days after bayessbw’s pupation date and 17.5 days after BioSIM’s, a pupal period plus a few days of adult maturation in either case. The two intervals differ by the models’ disagreement on the pupation date itself (Table 26), not by anything about the pupal stage. The standard deviation of about six days is the part worth pursuing: if it is structured by temperature rather than random, it is a pupal development function waiting to be fitted.

6.4 Would a degree-day pupal stage help?

A constant is a poor model of a poikilotherm’s development, so the obvious improvement on the fixed 12.9 d interval is to accumulate degree-days from pupation and predict the catch median when a threshold is reached. R/06_pupal_lag_test.R fits that and compares it with the constant.

The degree-day model wins by 0.08 days out of sample, on 170 locality-years. The fitted base ran to the bottom of the grid, which is the diagnostic rather than a detail: at a base of 0 °C the accumulation is nearly linear in mean temperature, which is as close as the model can come to collapsing back into the constant. Over the whole dataset it stretches the interval from 11 to 16 days, against a residual scatter of six.

6.5 Why no development function would help

A development model can only use temperature, so two numbers bound what it could ever achieve.

The interval does not respond to the temperature the pupae experienced: the correlation is −0.04, where a development model needs a strong negative, and the best smooth function of that temperature explains 6% of the variance. It is instead a property of the site: 64% of its variance sits between localities against 12% between years, and a per-locality constant cuts the scatter from 6.4 to 3.8 days.

Worse for the development explanation, the sign is backwards. The interval grows with July temperature (+0.47) and falls with latitude (−0.39): the warm southern sites, where development should be fastest, are the ones whose catch arrives longest after predicted pupation. A pupal stage would shorten the interval exactly where the data need it lengthened.

6.6 What the long intervals look like

A quarter of the catch, on average, falls after the modelled cohort has finished flying, and that share is what distinguishes the long-interval sites (r = 0.72). It is also a southern phenomenon (r = −0.46 with latitude). The nightly curves show what that means.

The short-interval sites catch their moths inside the modelled window and then stop. At the long-interval sites the catch is displaced: 62% of it falls after the window against 13% elsewhere, essentially none before it, and at Brunswick Township in 1981 the entire season’s catch — 99% — arrives after the model says flight has ended.

The width, though, is unchanged: 11.4 days from p05 to p95 against 10.9 days for the rest. A same-width curve arriving late is exactly what a slower pupal stage would produce, which is why the result of Section 6.4 is worth restating carefully. The problem is not that the delay is implausible; it is that the delay is not a function of temperature. It is a property of the site, and it is largest at the warmest sites, where a development model must run faster rather than slower.

Millinocket in 1980 is the instructive exception: catch through the modelled window and a separate spike a fortnight after it. Two modes are what an influx on top of a resident population should look like, and a systematic search for them across the 170 curves has not been done.

6.7 Latitude, or how many moths were caught?

The offset’s spatial structure could be something simpler than geography: a percentile estimated from a few hundred moths is a poorer statistic than one estimated from twenty thousand, and the sites that fit worst are also sites that catch little. Latitude and catch size turn out to be nearly independent here (r = 0.22 across locality-years), so the two can be separated.

Both terms are significant and mostly independent: latitude carries four times the unique variance of catch size. The next table asks the sharper question — is this about which localities, or about which years at a locality?

A locality’s poor years are not its low-catch years: within a site the offset does not follow the size of the catch. The effect is between localities — a property of which sites, not of how many moths a given season produced.

The two effects add. Latitude is visible at either catch level and catch size at either latitude, and the interaction is marginal (p = 0.039): the catch effect is somewhat stronger in the south. Restricted to catches of 1,000 moths or more, the latitude gradient survives at about 2.5 d per degree against 3.6 d per degree overall, while the catch effect disappears (r = 0.05).

The worst-fitting sites are both southern and habitually small-catch, so their offsets cannot be assigned to either cause alone. Southern localities that caught in the thousands sit far closer to the model.

6.8 Is the catch-size effect precision, or biology?

Part of it is precision. The spread of the offset is about twice as wide at small catches as at large ones — sd 7.3 d below a thousand moths against 4.5 d above five thousand — which is what estimating a percentile from few moths does.

Precision alone, though, produces scatter, not a shift, and a detection threshold — the mechanism that would produce one — makes a specific prediction: it should clip the sparse early nights, delaying the observed start and narrowing the observed curve. The data go the other way.

Small catches carry proportionally more of their catch after the modelled window, not less before it, and their curves are slightly wider. That is the opposite of clipping, and it is the same signature as the displaced southern curves of Section 6.4.

It also sharpens the immigration hypothesis into something testable. If the late weight came from moths arriving rather than from the local cohort, it should matter most where the local population is small — which is what the negative correlation with catch size says — and those late nights should coincide with conditions that carry moths, which the extracted wind fields can be asked directly. The alternative reading is that a small catch reflects a site marginal for the insect, where the local cohort is both sparse and genuinely late; distinguishing the two needs the nightly weather, not more summary statistics.

6.9 Open questions for the comparison

  • The spatial residual is the next problem, and neither the weather nor the missing pupal stage explains it. Latitude is a proxy, not an explanation. The two models run on different weather and make the same spatial error, and Section 6.4 rules out a temperature-driven pupal stage as the missing piece. What is left is what both models share — development with no site-level host, shading or microclimate modifier — and what neither contains: immigration. Section 6.4 narrows it further: the southern catch curves are displaced late by a week or more at unchanged width, so whatever is missing acts like a site-fixed delay rather than a broadening. Section 7 narrows it again, and changes its shape: the observed dates carry almost no latitudinal gradient while both models impose one of about four days per degree, so this is a gradient-slope error rather than a southern site effect.
  • Trap attraction is not modelled at all. The observed curve is a catch curve. Nightly weather gates flight and gates trapping, and neither is in the comparison yet; the hourly CaSR variables extracted for every locality-year — temperature, wind, precipitation — were extracted for exactly this purpose.
  • The comparable set could be larger. Relaxing the tail threshold from 5% to 10% would return 12 further records and the years 1987 and 1988; whether the added truncation is acceptable is a judgement the sensitivity table in Section 2 supports.

7 Is flight synchronous across Maine?

Section 6 leaves both models early in the south, and Section 6.4 rules out a missing pupal stage as the cause. That leaves a site-level effect neither model contains, and immigration — a locality’s catch need not be its own cohort. R/07_flight_synchrony.R tests the second without using weather at all, by asking whether southern catches happen on the region’s dates or on their own. Two predictions separate the explanations: a wave of moths arriving from the north would flatten the latitudinal gradient in catch dates, and at nightly resolution it would make distant localities spike on the same calendar nights.

7.1 The latitudinal gradient

Over the 3.8 degrees of latitude the trap network spans, the observed median catch date moves by 2.5 days; BioSIM moves it by 16.0 and bayessbw by 11.5. The observed gradient is not distinguishable from zero, and it stays flat on the best-sampled records while BioSIM’s stays steep on the same rows.

Averaged over those 16 years the southern localities catch their moths 1.9 days before the northern ones; the model puts them 6.7 days ahead. Seasonal timing across the network is, to within a couple of days, the same everywhere.

This reframes the residual of Section 6. What looked like a southern site effect is a gradient-slope error: both models spread flight across Maine about seven times more than the catches do, and the offset we were measuring is the difference between a steep modelled gradient and a flat observed one. It also explains why both models show it despite running on different weather, and why the worst sites are the extreme ones.

7.2 Nightly synchrony

A flat seasonal gradient is consistent with immigration, but also with a regionally synchronous emergence that the models exaggerate. The nightly curves separate the two: arriving moths should make distant localities spike together.

Over all 1282 pairs the median correlation is 0.20 against a shuffled-year null of -0.04, and 21% of pairs exceed 0.5 against 6% in the null. So same-night synchrony is real. It is also local:

Synchrony decays with distance, and the north–south pairs are the weakest of the three types despite having the same null. The best lag is zero days for every pair type, so there is no systematic delay of the kind transport would impose.

That is the opposite of what a northward wave delivering the southern catch would produce. What the nightly data show is nearby traps sharing flight nights — local weather gating flight and trappability — and southern traps sharing few nights with northern ones.

7.3 What this says about immigration

The hypothesis survives at the seasonal scale and fails at the nightly one. The more parsimonious reading of both results is that real flight across Maine is nearly synchronous and that both development models exaggerate how strongly latitude and temperature spread it: the gradient is wrong, rather than the southern catch being foreign.

One caveat keeps immigration alive: arrivals need not be simultaneous across localities, because the wind fields differ from night to night, so weak north–south nightly correlation is not proof of absence.

A second candidate — that the gradient is really topography, since BioSIM was run with elev = NaN and the CaSR extraction carries no terrain — is tested in Section 7.4 below and ruled out.

That leads directly to a test of how much site-specific weather is buying us at all, which is Section 7.6 below: if flight is regionally synchronous, one regional weather series should predict the catches about as well as a model run at each trap’s own coordinates.

7.4 Is the gradient an elevation error?

Elevation is the obvious suspect for a gradient that is too steep. R/03 leaves it unspecified, so BioSIM takes it from its own digital elevation model, and elevation is itself a latitude proxy in this network: the southern localities are coastal lowlands and the northern ones sit above 300 m (median 68 m against 303 m, r = 0.56 with latitude). R/08_elevation_check.R fetches an elevation for every locality from the USGS 3DEP point-query service — 7 to 573 m, median 218 — and asks BioSIM the same question twice, once with its own elevation model and once with the measured value.

Elevation does move the model. Over the plausible range of 100 to 500 m the flight date shifts by -1.9 d per 100 m at Blue Hill Township and +1.2 d per 100 m at Clayton Lake, against a run-to-run noise of about a tenth of a day. The two signs are not a typo: at the coastal locality a higher assumed elevation brings flight earlier, which cannot be a lapse rate and suggests that elevation also enters BioSIM’s choice and weighting of source weather stations — coastal stations at low elevation have cool summers. The mechanism is not established here; what matters is that the model is demonstrably sensitive.

BioSIM’s elevation model is already right at these localities. Supplying the measured value moves the flight date by a few tenths of a day — of the same order as the replicate-to-replicate variation of the service itself — leaves the mean offset against the catches where it was, and does not touch the gradient, which stays near six days per degree against an observed tenth of a day. A full re-run with elevation, one switch in R/03, would not change any conclusion in this log, so it has not been made.

7.5 How precisely does the location have to be right?

The elevation work turned up something that does matter. A modelled date at a coastal locality is not a smooth function of where the point is: displacing the same trap eastwards in steps, with BioSIM’s own elevation model each time, moves the answer by three days inside the first kilometre and then wanders back.

That is not a lapse rate or a distance effect; it is what a discrete set of source weather stations looks like when a point crosses from one interpolation neighbourhood into another. Two consequences. A modelled date cannot be attributed to a trap more finely than a few days at a coastal site, which matters because the recorded coordinates in this dataset carry a stated uncertainty of one to eight kilometres — though that uncertainty does not predict the size of the offset (Section 6), so this behaves as noise rather than as a bias. And a locality must always be queried at its recorded coordinates: an earlier version of this work used a coordinate rounded to two decimals from memory, landed 1.5 km away, and read that as evidence that BioSIM’s elevation model was wrong at the coast. It was not.

7.6 Does site-specific weather help at all?

If flight is as synchronous as Section 7 suggests, a model driven by one regional weather series — a single prediction per year, the same for every locality — should predict the catches about as well as the site-specific runs. R/09_regional_weather_test.R builds that comparison. The regional BioSIM run is one point at the centroid of the trap network (45.64 °N, 69.12 °W); the regional bayessbw run is the same simulation as Section 6.4 driven by the hourly temperature averaged over all localities. Each predictor is given one intercept, fitted on the other years, so a constant bias is not charged against any of them and none is scored on its own year.

Site-specific weather does not merely fail to help. It makes both models worse. Replacing the site-specific run with a single regional series changes the error by -2.18 days for BioSIM and -1.60 days for bayessbw, and raises the correlation with the observed dates from 0.49 to 0.67 and from 0.40 to 0.52. One number per year beats a model run at each trap’s own coordinates.

The last line of the table is the floor: the mean observed date of the other localities trapped in the same year, which is what a perfect regional predictor would look like. At 3.80 days it is only 0.59 days better than regional BioSIM, so the regional run already captures most of the predictable signal, and what the site-specific runs add on top of it is error.

Two caveats on the comparison. The regional predictors cannot capture real site-to-site variation, because they are constant within a year — the result is not that no such variation exists, but that it is smaller than the error the models make when they try to represent it. And averaging temperature before running a development model is not the same as averaging the development of each site, since the rate curves are non-linear; the regional bayessbw run is a model of the average weather, not an average of the models.

Taken with Section 7 this is the practical conclusion of the comparison. For predicting when spruce budworm flies in Maine, the useful signal in these models is the year, not the site; and a phenology model applied at a single trap’s coordinates will be wrong by about six days, mostly because it imposes a latitudinal gradient the moths do not follow. Section 8 turns that finding into a predictive model and measures what it can do.

8 Predicting the nightly catch curve

Everything so far has compared summary dates. This section asks the predictive question directly: given a development model, how well can the shape of a season be predicted at a locality — the share of its catch falling on each night?

Abundance is deliberately not predicted. Nothing in this project forecasts population density, so every model below carries one free level per locality-year that absorbs the season total and leaves only timing to explain. A Poisson likelihood with such a level per group is a multinomial over that group’s nights, so the fitted values read directly as predicted shares, and a held-out locality-year needs no level of its own.

R/10_nightly_count_model.R fits 9 such models to 7,481 trapped nights from 203 locality-years (50% of nights caught nothing) and scores them leave-one-year-out.

The two bayessbw rows need no lag constant. The correction is a spline in days from the driving curve’s own median, so the interval between pupation and the catch is fitted rather than assumed — which is what made the shifted series on Figure 1 uninformative about level and is repaired here.

Four things come out of that table.

A calibrated regional curve is the best predictor, and it is a usable one: 3.2 days of mean absolute error on the median catch date, a bias of -0.2 days, and 80% of locality-years inside five days — all out of sample, and with no information from the year being predicted.

BioSIM’s raw site curve does no better than climatology. Used as delivered it ties a seasonal average fitted from other years on mean absolute error (4.47 d against 4.48 d) and is worse on the two metrics that penalise large misses and mis-placed nightly mass: RMSE 5.82 d against 5.30 d, and a mean log predicted share of −3.38 against −3.35. Its bias is the largest of any specification at −2.19 d. Giving the curve a free exponent helps, a shape correction does not, and replacing the site curve with the single regional one helps most. Latitude makes things worse again, for the fourth time in this log.

The pupation distribution does not do better than the flight curve. Applied locality by locality it lands where BioSIM’s site curve does (4.85 days against 4.58), and the regional bayessbw run is the weaker of the two (4.25 days) — the opposite of BioSIM, where going regional helped most. Both bayessbw specifications are almost unbiased, which is the spline absorbing the pupation-to-catch interval as intended, but they are less sharp: a mean log predicted share of -3.27 and -3.34 against -2.99 for the best. The two development models differ by about four days in the pupation date, but that offset is nearly constant and the calibration absorbs it, so this is not a disagreement about the date; it is that bayessbw’s year-to-year placement carries less of the signal the catches follow, consistent with its weaker year-mean correlation in Table 29.

Almost all of the shape is empirical. The fitted exponent on the regional curve is 0.24, so the modelled curve enters the prediction heavily damped. reg-med settles how much it is worth by removing it altogether and keeping only the spline in days from its median: that costs nothing on timing (3.21 days of mean absolute error against 3.21, the same 80% inside five days) and a little on the nightly likelihood (-3.05 against -2.99 per moth). So what the development model contributes is when the season is centred — which year runs early, which runs late — and the curve’s own form adds only a marginal sharpening of the nightly fit.

Measured on the trapped nights, where the fit is supported, the correction moves the predicted median +2.8 days relative to BioSIM’s curve as delivered, with a spread of 5.7 days across locality-years, and it widens the predicted central 90% from 13.9 to 15.8 days. The observed central 90% is 11.2 days, so the calibrated prediction is well centred and too broad. Part of that gap is not model error: the observed width is one realisation of a very overdispersed count and a spiky realisation is narrower than the mean curve behind it. Section 10 measures it properly by simulating realisations, and the over-width survives at about two and a half days rather than the five this comparison suggests.

Calibration removes most of the spatial structure: the residual’s correlation with latitude falls to -0.15 from the +0.49 of Section 6. A southern excess survives — mean absolute error 3.7 days against 2.8 in the north — so the gradient is corrected on average rather than explained.

8.1 What this model is and is not good for

It predicts timing, out of sample, to about three days on the median and within five days four times out of five. That is enough to say when a flight season will be centred at a Maine locality given the year’s weather, which is the operational question. Its predicted spread is too wide by about half again, so a prediction interval taken straight from the fitted curve will be conservative.

It does not predict how many moths will be caught: the season total is an input, not an output. It also does not separate flight from trappability. Nightly weather is absent by design, and the model’s own diagnostics show where that would pay: 50% of nights caught nothing, and the count variance is several thousand times the mean, so the nightly residual is dominated by night-to-night variation that a development model cannot address. Temperature, wind and precipitation at each locality-night are already extracted and would enter this model as covariates without changing anything else about it.

One technical caveat for anyone refitting: the correction spline is a natural spline in days from the modelled median, and its behaviour beyond about 0b115 days rests on few nights — the upturn at the far right of the fitted correction is an edge artefact, not a second flight period.

9 What distribution describes a night’s catch?

The marginal distribution of nightly counts is not a useful target: these nights differ enormously in what they should hold, from a locality-year totalling a hundred moths to one totalling seventy thousand, and within a season from the first night of flight to the peak. The question worth asking is conditional — given what a night is expected to hold, how is the count scattered around it?

R/11_count_distribution.R gives every candidate the same mean structure, the reg+ predictor of Section 8 with a locality-year level, and varies only the distribution of the count around that mean.

Observed: 3,715 zero-catch nights of 7,481, and a largest count of 27,500 moths.

The Poisson is hopeless, by 2,506,893 AIC. It expects 1099 empty nights where 3,715 occurred. The raw variance-to-mean ratio of the catches is 6,697.

Zero inflation is unnecessary. Adding a zero-inflation component to the negative binomial costs two AIC and moves nothing — the fitted component is essentially empty, and the simulated number of empty nights is unchanged. The empty nights are the lower tail of a very overdispersed count distribution, not a separate process that switches the trap off. That is worth stating plainly, because a zero-inflated model is the reflex for trap data with a quarter of its nights empty.

The variance is quadratic in the mean, and the negative binomial has it right. Binning nights by their expected catch gives an empirical variance-mean slope of 1.83 on the log scale, where 1 is the Poisson and nbinom1 and 2 is the negative binomial (NB2). nbinom1, which forces slope 1, is beaten by 1,308 AIC, and NB2’s fitted variance function tracks the binned data across three orders of magnitude (Figure 5).

The Poisson-lognormal wins the likelihood but not the second moment. A Poisson count whose mean carries a lognormal nightly multiplier fits better by 159 AIC and reproduces the number of empty nights most closely (3543 against 3,715, where NB2 gives 3685). Its fitted multiplier has a lognormal standard deviation of 2.76 on the log scale, which implies a variance inflation of 1979 times the squared mean against the 5.3 the data show — about 376 times too much. Its simulated largest count is 801,923 moths against 27,500 observed, where NB2 simulates 100,658.

Both statements can hold at once because a lognormal mixture this wide is extremely right-skewed: most nights sit near its median, which is what the likelihood rewards, while its mean and variance are carried by rare enormous nights that the data do not contain.

9.1 The answer, and what it is for

  • For describing or predicting nightly catches — regression, prediction intervals, simulation — the negative binomial (NB2) is the distribution best adapted to these data: variance 5.3 times the squared mean on top of the Poisson term, matching the empirical variance-mean relation across three orders of magnitude, with the better-behaved upper tail.
  • The Poisson-lognormal is the better description of the bulk and the more interpretable mechanism — nightly catchability as a multiplicative random factor — but its second moment and tail are wrong, so it should not be used to simulate extremes.
  • Do not zero-inflate. The empty nights need no separate mechanism.
  • Neither family should be trusted for extreme quantiles: both overstate the largest catches.

Whichever is used, the size of the nightly term is the finding worth carrying forward. A standard deviation of the nightly multiplier of 2.3 times the mean under NB2 — an order of magnitude in each direction under the lognormal — dwarfs everything the development models disagree about: a ten-day error in the modelled median changes a given night’s expected catch by less than the night-to-night noise. It also explains the shape of these curves directly. A third of a season’s catch arriving on its single best night (Section 6.4) is not a curious feature of spruce budworm flight; it is what a nightly multiplier of this size produces on a seasonal curve of ordinary width.

One caveat on the fitting. glmmTMB warns that it was built against a different version of TMB than the one installed here. The two leading fits were therefore repeated with lme4 — the Poisson-lognormal as an observation-level random effect, the negative binomial through glmer.nb — which reproduced the log-likelihoods to within 3 AIC and the nightly standard deviation to three decimals, so the ranking does not rest on that warning.

10 Forecasting from what a forecast has

The sections above ask what the models get right. This one fixes the inputs a forecast would actually have for a locality-year and asks how well the flight season can be predicted from them:

  1. a distribution of developmental dates — pupation from bayessbw, or adult emergence from BioSIM;
  2. hourly temperature at the locality;
  3. the season’s total catch.

No trap data from the year being predicted. The season total being an input is what makes this tractable: abundance is not modelled, only the share of that total falling on each night.

10.1 The distribution of adult dates

BioSIM’s Adults column, kept in Section 4, is a stock — it re-counts the same individuals every day and sums to about 1,500% of the cohort, so it is not a distribution. The series that is one is MaleEmergence + FemaleEmergence, which sums to exactly 100%. At the regional point in 1978 it is centred on day 190.4 with a central 90% of 13.2 days, against 194.7 and 14.4 days for the flight curve: emergence is four days earlier and slightly narrower, as it should be. This section is the first use of it.

10.2 Nightly temperature

Flight is crepuscular, so temperature is averaged over the hours 20:00 to 02:00 of each trap-night, with the hours after midnight assigned to the night that began the previous evening. Every one of the 7,481 trapped nights has a complete window.

10.3 Timing and nightly skill

For the median date, the two BioSIM series are interchangeable and better than bayessbw. The flight curve gives 3.23 days of mean absolute error and emergence 3.44 — a difference of a sixth of a day, so either BioSIM input can be used. Pupation from bayessbw costs about a day (4.93 d), and a seasonal spline with temperature but no development model at all is no better (4.82 d).

Nightly temperature does not help the median, but it is the first thing that has improved the nightly numbers. Adding it moves the median error the wrong way by a tenth of a day, while the log score per moth improves from -2.962 to -2.901 with the flight curve and from -3.061 to -2.945 with emergence. Temperature decides which nights inside the season the moths fly, not where the season sits — which is what the phenology is for.

10.4 The predicted season is genuinely too wide

Earlier sections compared the predicted mean curve’s central 90% with the observed one and called the prediction over-dispersed. That comparison is not quite fair: the observed width is measured on a single realisation of a very overdispersed count, and a spiky realisation is narrower than the smooth mean curve behind it. The check below simulates realisations from each fitted predictive distribution and measures their widths exactly as the observed width is measured.

Sampling noise accounts for about a day of the gap — the mean curve of the best specification spans 13.6 days and its realisations 13.2 — but the observed 11.2 days is still about two and a half days narrower than that, and only 76% of locality-years fall inside the simulated band where 90% should. So the over-width is real, and smaller than the figure quoted in Section 8: the honest statement is a realisation of 13.2 days against 11.2 observed, not the mean curve’s 13.6.

The nightly predictive intervals are correspondingly conservative: the 90% negative binomial interval, with the season total supplied, contains the observed count on 93% of nights.

10.5 Where this leaves the forecast

The one clear deficiency is the width. Every driver produces a season two to five days too broad, and the ranking of drivers by width follows their ranking by timing, which suggests a common cause: the shape correction is fitted across all locality-years and cannot know that a particular season will be compressed. A scale parameter on the fitted shape — sharpening the predicted curve by a factor estimated out of sample — is the obvious next step and has not been tried.

11 A callable predictor

R/13_fit_flight_predictor.R fits the model on every year and stores what is needed to predict a locality-year that was never trapped; R/functions/predict_flight.R consumes it. The call takes the three forecast inputs and nothing else:

source("daily_dynamics/R/functions/predict_flight.R")

out <- predict_flight(
  dev_curve    = emergence_1978,   # data frame: doy, pct
  hourly_temp  = weather_1978,     # data frame: datetime, Temp
  season_total = 12000,            # moths caught that season
  driver       = "emergence"       # or "flight", or "pupation"
)

It returns one row per night: the share of the season expected that night, the expected count, and a negative binomial predictive interval. Three driver variants are stored, so whichever developmental distribution is to hand can be used — BioSIM’s flight or emergence curve, or bayessbw’s pupation distribution.

The shares are normalised over the nights supplied, so the answer is always of this season’s catch, how much falls on each of these nights. A window shorter than the flight season inflates every share, exactly as a trap that operates for part of the season does.

11.1 Sharpening, and the trade-off it forces

Section 10 leaves the predicted season two to five days too broad. The fitted shape is a log-share curve, so raising it to a power κ > 1 sharpens it around its own peak without moving the peak. κ is chosen out of sample by stacking: for each year it is the value that scores best on the other years’ held-out predictions.

The two criteria disagree, and the disagreement is the useful part.

By the log score, no sharpening at all. κ = 1 for every driver: the proper scoring rule for nightly counts prefers the broad curve, because sharpening moves mass away from the shoulders where a handful of moths still arrive, and the log score punishes that heavily.

By width, κ between 1.25 and 1.51, and it works almost exactly: with the flight curve the width error falls from +2.33 days to +0.42 days. The cost is a tenth of a day on the median (3.25 → 3.26) and 0.053 on the log score per moth.

So the choice depends on the use. For when to expect flight and over what window — the operational question — sharpen: the season comes out the right length at a negligible cost in the median. For probabilistic statements about a particular night’s count, leave κ = 1. predict_flight() defaults to the sharpened setting and takes kappa = "logscore" or a number to override.

11.2 A worked example

The left panel is the largest catch in the dataset, 71,730 moths over 44 nights; its median is predicted -1.9 days out, and the right panel’s +3.4 days. The temperature term is visible in both: the sharp dips are cold nights, and the observed catches dip with them — day 187 at East Allagash averaged 6.9 °C through the flight hours and caught one moth, where the neighbouring warm nights caught hundreds.

The intervals are wide, and honestly so: with θ = 0.19 a night expected to yield a thousand moths has a 90% interval running from a few dozen to several thousand. That is the nightly variability measured in Section 9, not a defect of the phenology.

11.3 What it does not do

  • It does not predict abundance: the season total is an input. Predicting that needs a population model, which nothing in this project provides.
  • It has no site term, by design — Section 7.6 showed site-specific weather makes the timing worse, and every latitude term tried has hurt.
  • It inherits the southern excess of Section 8: localities below 45.5 °N are fitted about a day worse than northern ones.
  • Its inputs must be regional: the fitted variants use BioSIM run once at the network centroid. Feeding it a curve from a site-specific run is a different input from the one it was calibrated on.

12 The missing nights are censoring

An m night is not a night whose catch is unknown in the way a lottery number is unknown. It is a night inside a running trapping period whose catch was not recorded, and because flight is a seasonal curve, where the night falls decides which part of that curve is unidentified. R/01_read_trap_data.R therefore reads them as censoring: a missing night before 15 July bounds the rise of the season (left-censored), a missing night after it bounds the decline (right-censored). The side is carried on every night in trap_daily$censoring and counted per record in n_cens_left / n_cens_right.

Of the 30 missing nights in the working dataset, 0 are left-censored and 30 right-censored, spread over 4 records. A further 1 record was removed from the dataset because of where its censored nights fell (below).

Left-censoring has disappeared from the dataset, and not by accident: the large June blocks of m codes fall before the first capture of their year, so the season window of Section 2 excludes them along with the rest of the out-of-season range. Every censored night that survives is in the declining tail.

12.1 The side is not the magnitude

A censored night costs what the season was doing on it, and those two blocks of twelve mid-June nights in 1983 cost nothing at all — nothing was flying. R/14_censoring.R makes that quantitative: for each affected record the fitted predictor (Section 11) is given the record’s own night set, counted and censored together, and asked how much of the season it expects on the nights with no count. The percentiles are then re-estimated with those nights completed at their expected level, and the difference is the bias that treating a censored night as simply absent introduces.

The distribution is extremely skewed. Across the records retained in the dataset the median has 0.02% of its season inside censored nights, and only 0 of 4 assessed records exceed 1%, the largest reaching 0.0%. One record was far outside that range and was excluded on the strength of it (below).

One record was removed from the dataset rather than flagged. Elliotsville Township in 1978 has only two censored nights — 8 and 9 July — but they sit at the peak, and the predictor expects 26% of the whole season on them: 3,205 moths against the 9,060 recorded. Completing them moves its median catch date +1.2 days and p95 -0.9 days. That is not a flight curve with a gap in it but one missing its peak, so no percentile taken from it is identifiable, and exclude_records in R/01_read_trap_data.R drops it. Its nights are kept in data/processed/trap_excluded.rds so this diagnostic — the one that justified the decision — still reports it.

The record passed usable_phenology and flight_complete throughout, because neither flag looks at where a gap falls relative to the catch. That is a limitation of those flags: a censored peak is invisible to them.

The two right-censored 1983 records behave as expected for a gap in the declining tail: Hay Lake’s p95 moves +0.1 days with the median untouched. Steuben 1989 is the smallest season in the group ( moths) and its five late-June nights shift the median days.

One record could not be assessed: Meddybemps Township in 1987 has no regional emergence curve, 1987 being one of the three years with no comparable locality-year.

12.2 The published aggregates do not move

The median model-observation offset is unchanged at -2.12 days and the observed latitudinal gradient moves from +0.656 to +0.656 days per degree north. Three materially affected records out of 203 cannot move a median, and the gradient conclusion of Section 7 survives untouched.

So the censoring rule changes no result reported here. What it changes is what may be done next: a record whose peak is censored should not contribute to a width or late-tail analysis at face value, and censoring now makes those records findable instead of leaving them indistinguishable from complete ones. The diagnostic is deliberately not a correction — nothing downstream reads the completed percentiles.

13 Findings so far

13.1 The data

226 Maine light-trap records from the Rhainds compilation cover 49 localities and 22 years (1968–1989), with 8,286 counted trap-nights, every record above 99 moths for the season. The minimum-effort rule of Section 2 marks 223 records as usable for percentile phenology; intersected with the modelled cohorts that finish flight, 203 locality-years carry a meaningful model-versus-observed comparison. Hourly CaSR weather was extracted for all 226 locality-years (1.99 million hours).

13.2 Two development models that agree on the pattern, not the date

BioSIM’s Spruce_Budworm_Biology and the Bayesian model of bayessbw were fitted to different data, by different methods, and were driven by different weather — BioSIM’s own station network against the CaSR grid. They rank locality-years alike (r = 0.78), but BioSIM pupates a median 4.0 days earlier (Table 26), so the observed median catch follows predicted pupation by 13.4 d for bayessbw and 17.5 d for BioSIM. In the pupation model, individual variation exceeds parameter uncertainty about fourfold: a population takes 9.3 days to pupate from p05 to p95, while the posterior places its median to within 2.2 days.

13.3 The central finding

Against the catches, modelled flight is early by a median 2.1 days at p50 (3.7 d at p05, 1.0 d at p95). That average hides a split: year means correlate at 0.84, but within a year across localities the correlation is 0.20.

The reason is a gradient-slope error. Both models spread flight across Maine about seven times more steeply with latitude than the catches do (Table 41): +0.66 days per degree observed, against +4.17 (BioSIM) and +2.99 (bayessbw) — 2.5 days of observed spread across the network against 16.0 and 11.5 modelled. Flight in Maine is essentially synchronous, and the apparent “early in the south” offset is the difference between a steep modelled gradient and a flat real one. The two models’ offsets correlate at 0.71, locality-year by locality-year, which is why the same error appears in both.

13.4 Five explanations tested and set aside

Catch size survives as a second, weaker and near-independent site covariate: +1.43 days per tenfold catch against +3.35 days per degree of latitude, and with no effect within a locality.

13.5 What predicts the flight season

Site-specific weather makes both models worse than a single regional series (Table 47). Built into the nightly count model of Section 8, the calibrated regional curve predicts a held-out year’s median catch date to 3.21 days of mean absolute error, bias -0.24 d, with 80% of locality-years inside five days — against 5.09 days for a seasonal climatology.

Two qualifications matter for using it. First, the development model contributes the date, not the shape: with an exponent of 0.24 on the modelled curve, deleting the curve entirely and keeping only its median plus the empirical correction costs nothing on timing (3.21 days). BioSIM’s uncorrected site curve, meanwhile, buys nothing over climatology — it ties on mean absolute error and is worse on RMSE, on the nightly likelihood and on bias. Second, the calibrated prediction is over-dispersed: it widens the predicted central 90% to 15.8 days against 11.2 observed, so an interval read straight off the fitted curve is conservative.

The distribution around that prediction is also settled (Section 9): a night’s catch is negative binomial with a variance about 5.3 times the squared mean, it needs no zero inflation, and the implied night-to-night multiplier varies by an order of magnitude in each direction — more than anything the development models disagree about.

bayessbw’s pupation distribution does not improve on this (4.85 d site-specific, 4.25 d regional). Its value in this project is as the independent check on pupation timing, not as the driver of the prediction.

13.6 A predictor that can be called

predict_flight() (Section 11) packages the result into the three inputs that will be available at prediction time: a developmental distribution, hourly temperature, and the season total. On held-out years it places the median catch date within about three days and, with the sharpening parameter set by width, returns a season of the right length. It predicts shares of a given total, never the total itself.

13.7 What is still open

  • Wind and precipitation are still unused. Nightly temperature is now in the model (Section 10) and it is the one covariate that improves the nightly numbers, but it does not move the median; wind and precipitation are already extracted per locality-night and would enter the same way.
  • Immigration is not excluded, only unsupported at the nightly scale. Arrivals need not be simultaneous across localities, and no systematic search for second modes has been made across the 203 curves. Millinocket in 1980 (Figure 2) is the one panel that looks like an influx.
  • The southern excess survives calibration. The count model’s residual correlates only -0.15 with latitude, but southern localities are still fitted about a day worse than northern ones, so the gradient is corrected on average rather than explained.
  • Abundance is not modelled at all. Every result here is about timing; the season total is an input to the predictive model, never an output.
